waste-hierarchy.title: The waste hierarchy
waste-hierarchy.lede: The waste hierarchy is how the EU ranks what to do with waste, from best to worst for the environment. Here is where the EU's municipal waste went in {year}.

municipal-waste.title: How much waste do we generate?
municipal-waste.key_message: In {year}, the EU generated about {eu_mt} million tonnes of municipal waste, about {eu_kg} kg per person.
municipal-waste.lede: Municipal waste is the waste from our homes, plus similar waste from shops and offices.
municipal-waste.try: Find your country: is its bar longer or shorter than the EU27 bar? {n_above} countries are above it.

decoupling.title: Can the economy grow without more waste?
decoupling.key_message: Mostly yes: since 2011 the EU's economy grew by {gdp_growth}% per person, but waste per person by only {waste_growth}%.
decoupling.lede: When the blue line (the economy) is above the orange line (waste), the economy has grown more than waste since 2011. In {n_absolute} countries, waste per person even fell while the economy grew.
decoupling.try: Search for the Netherlands: its economy grew, and its waste per person fell more than in any other country.

distance-to-target.title: Are we recycling enough?
distance-to-target.key_message: The EU-wide packaging rate is already above the 2025 target level, but the rates for municipal waste and plastic are still below it.
distance-to-target.lede: Each dot is a country's Eurostat recycling rate in {target_year}, two years before the deadline. Blue dots are at or above the 2025 target level; red and orange dots are below it.
distance-to-target.try: Find your country: is it at or above the 2025 target level for each type of waste?

waste-treatment.title: Where do our {eu_kg} kg of waste end up?
waste-treatment.key_message: Of the {eu_kg} kg each of us generated in {year}, about {recycling_kg} kg were recycled, {energy_kg} kg burnt for energy and {disposal_kg} kg disposed of.
waste-treatment.lede: Follow a year of municipal waste, per person, down the waste hierarchy. The wider the band, the more kilos go that way.
waste-treatment.try: Try Austria, which recycles the most per person, Malta, which landfills the most per person, and Denmark, which burns the most per person for energy.

distance_to_target.aria_label: Recycling rates in {target_year} by country and type of waste, compared with the 2025 targets

legend.axis: Points below or above the target

notes: Below the target in 2023 doesn't mean failing. Countries still had two years to go, and 8 countries postponed the municipal waste deadline (they must reach at least 50% by 2025). 8 countries postponed some packaging materials: Czechia (aluminium), Greece, Croatia and Hungary (plastic and glass), Luxembourg (plastic), Portugal (aluminium and glass), Sweden (glass) and Malta.

Poland changed how it measures in 2023: its treatment figures are now reported directly by companies instead of being partly estimated. Its recycling rate fell from 40.9% to 27.6% while its waste stayed the same, so 2023 cannot be compared with earlier years.
The municipal waste rate includes composting and, for some countries, preparing things for re-use.

Some packaging rates are above 100% (Slovenia, Poland), which makes them look further above the target than they are. Cyprus's steel rate (221.5%) is left out. Bulgaria, Czechia and Hungary have no packaging rates for 2023.

level_hover.prep_reuse: Things checked, cleaned or repaired so they can be used again. Second best, after not making the waste at all.
level_hover.recycling: Waste made into new materials, or into compost. Next best after preparing for re-use.
level_hover.energy_recovery: Burnt in plants that use the energy. Below recycling: the waste is burnt, not made into something new. Above disposal, where it is buried or burnt without using the energy.
level_hover.disposal: Mostly buried in landfill, or burnt without using the energy. The last option in the waste hierarchy.
level_hover.unaccounted: Counted when it was generated, but in no treatment figure. The data does not show what happened to it.
level_hover.unaccounted_eu: It includes the small amount prepared for re-use.

notes.reuse_missing_eu: There is no EU figure for preparing for re-use: Eurostat publishes none, and 8 countries do not report it. The little that is prepared for re-use is inside 'not in the figures'.
notes.reuse_missing_country: {name} does not report preparing for re-use, so that level is empty.
notes.not_accounted: Not in the figures: waste counted when it was generated, but in no treatment figure. The data does not say where it went.
notes.two_recycling: Recycling here ({recycling}% for the EU) leaves out preparing for re-use. Some countries count re-use in the recycling rate in the section above ({recycling_rate}%), which is why the two differ.

country_notes.PT: Portugal treated more waste than it generated in {year}, so it has no 'not in the figures' band. The data does not say why.
country_notes.PL: Poland changed how it measures in 2023: companies now report treatment directly, instead of it being partly estimated. That is why 21.5% of its waste is not in the figures. Its 2023 figures cannot be compared with earlier years.
country_notes.LV: Latvia has no disposal figure for 2023, so its chart has no disposal and no 'not in the figures' band, and is incomplete.

waste_treatment.about: Each band is a share of all municipal waste generated in {name} in {year}, turned into kg per person: the country's waste divided by its people. These are yearly averages, not what one household throws away. They include similar waste from businesses where a country counts it. Eurostat has no EU figure for landfill and burning without energy recovery in 2023, and Latvia has none either. I estimated both by adding up all 27 countries, using Latvia's 2022 figures.

closing.title: Recycling is only halfway up the waste hierarchy
closing.text: The EU recycles almost half of its municipal waste. Its EU-wide packaging rate is above the 2025 target level, but the rates for municipal waste and plastic are still below it. And the top of the waste hierarchy is generating less waste in the first place, and there the EU has hardly moved: about {eu_kg} kg per person, much as in 2011.

method_note.text: All figures come from Eurostat, the EU's statistics office: municipal waste (env_wasmun), packaging recycling (env_waspacr) and GDP per person (nama_10_pc). Each chart names its sources and the date I downloaded them. Figures in the texts are for 2023, the latest year with data for all 27 countries; the line chart goes up to 2024.

Czechia, Belgium, Austria, Slovakia and Luxembourg widened their definition to include similar waste from businesses: their waste per person jumped in one year without more waste being generated. Estonia and Slovenia added other waste, which partly explains their jumps. The EU figure includes these jumps.

method_note.lead: Some jumps have no known cause.
method_note.text: Waste per person fell sharply in Romania (2011) and Finland (2022 and 2023), and rose sharply in Latvia (2015). These changes are not explained; they should be checked with the countries.

The recycling rate (47.9% for the EU) also counts some preparing for re-use, as the target does. The waste hierarchy, and the chart of where each person's waste ends up, show recycling on its own (47.7%), with re-use as its own level, so nothing is counted twice.

method_note.lead: The waste hierarchy figures don't always add up to 100%.
method_note.text: Each level is a share of the waste generated, like the recycling targets. Some waste generated shows up in no treatment figure: 5.0% for the EU, and more than a tenth in 7 countries. I show it as 'not in the figures' rather than guess where it went. The EU's 2023 landfill and burnt-without-energy figures are my own estimate, as Latvia has no figure for them.

The 2025 recycling targets are set by EU law: 55% for municipal waste (Waste Framework Directive) and 65% for all packaging, with separate targets per material (Packaging and Packaging Waste Directive, now carried over by the new Packaging Regulation). 2023 is a snapshot two years before the deadline, and some countries legally postponed it.
GDP per person is adjusted for inflation (2020 prices). Ireland's GDP is pushed up by multinational companies, so its decoupling looks stronger than it is.

how_i_did_this.text: The data is downloaded from Eurostat's online data service (its API), so every figure can be traced back to the dataset it comes from, and each chart says when it was downloaded.

A chain of Python scripts takes the data through four layers: raw downloads (never edited), lookup tables (the EU countries, the recycling targets, the texts of this page), indicators built from each dataset, and the final tables this page reads. One command rebuilds everything in the right order and checks that only the 27 EU countries and the EU total reach the dashboard. Where a source value needed fixing, the fix is written down with its reason, and it stops applying if Eurostat corrects the value.

how_i_did_this.lead: A page built with D3 and React.
how_i_did_this.text: D3 does the maths (scales, lines, axes) and React draws the charts. The page is rebuilt and published on GitHub Pages every time the data or the code changes.

how_i_did_this.lead: Built with Claude and a team of AI agents.
how_i_did_this.text: The project was built with Claude Code, working with specialised agents: a data scientist that owns the pipeline and turns questions into checked findings; a data storyteller that shapes the story; a UX copywriter that writes the texts; a brand designer that proposed the visual identity; and a fact-checker that checks every text against the findings, and the findings against the data. Every text on this page may only use facts from the project's written findings, and every decision is logged in the project notes.
